title: Microsoft Graph API and the PowerShell SDK
monthTitle: Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale
summary: Understand what Microsoft Graph is, how it exposes Microsoft 365 and Intune as one REST API, and how to drive it from PowerShell with the Microsoft Graph SDK.
objectives: Describe Microsoft Graph as a single REST endpoint over Entra, Intune, and M365
Install the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK and its sub-modules
Authenticate with Connect-MgGraph using the right delegated scopes
Map a Graph REST endpoint to the equivalent Get-Mg* SDK cmdlet
Page through large result sets with -All instead of truncated pages
Call endpoints the SDK has no cmdlet for using Invoke-MgGraphRequest

options: A single REST API and endpoint that unifies Entra ID, Intune, and Microsoft 365 data
A local database on each device
quiz.why: Microsoft Graph is the unified REST API at graph.microsoft.com that exposes users, devices, Intune, mail, and more behind one consistent endpoint and permission model.

quiz.q: Which cmdlet authenticates a session and requests permission scopes for the Graph SDK?
quiz.why: Connect-MgGraph establishes the session; the -Scopes parameter requests the delegated permissions your subsequent calls require, following least privilege.

quiz.q: By default a Graph list call returns a limited page of results. How do you retrieve every item with an SDK cmdlet?
options: Run the cmdlet repeatedly until it errors
Pass the -All switch so the SDK follows the nextLink automatically
There is no way; Graph caps results
quiz.why: Graph paginates with an @odata.nextLink; the SDK's -All switch follows those links for you so you get the complete collection rather than just the first page.

quiz.q: When should you reach for Invoke-MgGraphRequest instead of a Get-Mg* cmdlet?
options: When you need a beta endpoint or one with no dedicated cmdlet, or full control over the raw request
quiz.why: Invoke-MgGraphRequest sends raw authenticated requests to any Graph URI, which is essential for beta endpoints, new features, or actions the typed cmdlets do not yet expose.

quiz.q: Name the command that lists which scopes (permissions) your current Graph session actually holds.
quiz.answer: (Get-MgContext).Scopes — Get-MgContext returns the active connection context including the granted Scopes, account, and tenant.
quiz.why: Checking Get-MgContext before troubleshooting saves time: a 403 is very often a missing scope rather than a code bug.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why request the narrowest set of scopes your script needs rather than broad ones?
quiz.answer: Least privilege limits the blast radius if credentials are misused and is required for security reviews and admin consent, so you ask only for the specific scopes the script's calls require.
quiz.why: Scopes are the permission model; requesting only what you need keeps consent prompts honest and reduces risk if the session or app is compromised.

body_markdown:
## One API over your whole tenant

**Microsoft Graph** is a single REST API, served from `https://graph.microsoft.com`, that exposes almost everything in your Microsoft cloud: **Entra ID** users and groups, **Intune** managed devices and policies, mail, Teams, and more. Instead of one module per product, you learn one endpoint, one permission model, and one query language (**OData**).

Everything is a resource at a URL. Users live at `/users`, managed devices at `/deviceManagement/managedDevices`, groups at `/groups`. Learn the URL pattern once and the whole API opens up.

## Installing and connecting the SDK

The **Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK** is a family of modules. Install the meta-module, or just the sub-modules you need to keep load times short.

```powershell
# Install once, for the current user
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph -Scope CurrentUser

# Or targeted sub-modules only
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.Authentication -Scope CurrentUser
Install-Module Microsoft.Graph.DeviceManagement -Scope CurrentUser
```

Authentication is **scope-based**. You ask only for the **delegated scopes** your script actually uses — this is least privilege, and reviewers will check it.

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All','User.Read.All'

# Confirm who you are and what you can do
(Get-MgContext).Scopes
```

If a call later returns **403 Forbidden**, your first suspect is a missing scope — check `Get-MgContext` before you blame your code.

## From REST endpoint to Get-Mg cmdlet

Every Graph endpoint maps to a typed cmdlet. The pattern is predictable: `GET /deviceManagement/managedDevices` becomes `Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice`.

```powershell
# Get every managed device, following pagination automatically
$devices = Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All

$devices |
    Where-Object { $_.OperatingSystem -eq 'Windows' } |
    Select-Object DeviceName, OsVersion, LastSyncDateTime
```

The **`-All`** switch matters. Without it, Graph returns just the first page and silently follows an `@odata.nextLink` for the rest; `-All` walks every page so you do not miss devices.

## OData query options keep payloads small

Do not pull whole objects and filter in PowerShell when Graph can do it server-side. Use `-Filter`, `-Select`, and `-Top`.

```powershell
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All `
    -Filter "operatingSystem eq 'Windows'" `
    -Property 'deviceName,osVersion,complianceState' |
    Select-Object DeviceName, OsVersion, ComplianceState
```

Server-side filtering means less data over the wire and fewer throttling problems on big tenants.

## Invoke-MgGraphRequest for anything the cmdlets miss

New features land in the **beta** endpoint first, and not every action has a typed cmdlet. **`Invoke-MgGraphRequest`** sends a raw authenticated request to any Graph URI and reuses your existing token.

```powershell
$uri = 'https://graph.microsoft.com/beta/deviceManagement/managedDevices?$top=5'
$response = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri $uri
$response.value | Select-Object deviceName, osVersion

# It also works for actions:
Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method POST `
    -Uri 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/managedDevices/{id}/rebootNow'
```

This is your escape hatch — when the SDK has no cmdlet, the REST call always works.

## Your task

Connect to Graph with the minimum scopes needed to read managed devices. Write a function `Get-IntuneDeviceInventory` that retrieves **all** managed devices with `-All`, uses server-side `-Filter` and `-Property` to return only Windows devices and only the `deviceName`, `osVersion`, and `lastSyncDateTime` fields, and exports the result to CSV. Then re-implement the same read using `Invoke-MgGraphRequest` against the v1.0 endpoint and confirm the two approaches return the same count.

slides.title: REST endpoint to Get-Mg cmdlet
bullets: Endpoints map to typed Get-Mg cmdlets.
GET /managedDevices becomes Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice.
The naming pattern is predictable.
Tab completion helps you find them.
slides.narration: Every Graph endpoint maps to a typed cmdlet, and the naming pattern is predictable. Get slash device management slash managed devices becomes Get dash M g Device Management Managed Device. Once you see the pattern, tab completion finds the rest. Here we grab managed devices into a variable and then select just the device name, O S version, and last sync time. Notice the dash All switch, which we will talk about next, because it is easy to get wrong.

slides.title: Pagination: always think -All
bullets: Graph returns one page by default.
It hides the rest behind @odata.nextLink.
-All follows every nextLink for you.
Without it you silently miss devices.
slides.code:
# first page only
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice
# every device
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All
slides.narration: Here is the gotcha that bites people. A Graph list call returns just the first page by default, maybe a hundred items, and hides the rest behind a link called at o data next link. If you forget the dash All switch, you silently miss devices and your report is wrong. With dash All, the S D K walks every page automatically and gives you the complete collection. On any list query against a real tenant, think dash All by default.

slides.title: OData: filter and select server-side
bullets: Use -Filter to filter on the server.
Use -Property to return only fields you need.
Less data over the wire, fewer throttles.
Do not pull everything then filter locally.
slides.narration: Do not drag entire objects across the network and then filter in PowerShell when Graph can do it for you. Use dash Filter to filter server side and dash Property to return only the fields you need. On a tenant with tens of thousands of devices this is the difference between a script that finishes in seconds and one that gets throttled and times out. Push the work to the server whenever you can.

slides.title: Invoke-MgGraphRequest: the escape hatch
bullets: Sends raw requests to any Graph URI.
Reuses your existing Connect-MgGraph token.
Reach for beta endpoints and missing cmdlets.
Works for GET and for POST actions alike.
slides.narration: Sometimes the typed cmdlets do not cover what you need. New features land in the beta endpoint first, and some actions simply have no cmdlet yet. Invoke dash M g Graph Request is your escape hatch. It sends a raw authenticated request to any Graph U R I and reuses the token from Connect dash M g Graph, so you do not handle auth again. It works for read calls and for action calls like reboot now. When in doubt, the raw REST call always works.
